title: I vibecoded a Minecraft clone in a week. Sort of.
author: Veelgez
selftext:
Well — "Minecraft clone" is the short version. It's closer to a voxel action-RPG: you see something on the horizon, you walk there, you fight, you carry stuff home and build with it. But it has blocks, you mine them, you place them, so let's not pretend.

I've been working on it for about **a week**. It's called **Fernweh** (working title — it's the German word for the ache to be somewhere far away). It's built in **Godot 4.7**, and yes, most of the code was written with an AI agent. I'll get into what that actually means further down, because I think that part is more interesting than the buzzword.

I'm posting this because I think the base is genuinely good now, and I want to start posting updates as it grows. **I'm planning to put out a playable build soon.**

# The one idea behind it

The moment I'm building everything around is seeing something on the horizon and deciding to go there.

That's surprisingly easy to lose. If your landmarks are procedurally rolled, they repeat, and after ten minutes they stop pulling you anywhere — you've seen the tower already, there's another one over there, who cares. So here it's flipped: **the terrain is generated, the reasons to go somewhere are not.** Infinite world, but the places in it are placed on purpose, and there are a finite number of them.

Second rule, and I'm strict about it: **what you have, you keep.** No gear that quietly becomes worthless because you walked into a different region. A biome locks you out because you don't have warm clothes yet — not because your number is too small.

# What's actually in it right now

**Combat.** Dodge roll with i-frames, hit-stop, input buffering, roll-cancel. Nine weapons including bare fists — from the dagger (14 damage, 4-hit chain, darts around) to the warhammer (70 damage, 1.3 s committed, two swings and someone's down). The classes actually behave differently: the axe hits three targets, the spear whiffs on things the sword connects with, the dagger does double damage from behind. Ten enemy types built from six body plans, with A\* pathing over walkable columns.

**The world.** Chunk streaming with no visible edge. Eight biomes with soft transitions — instead of "roll two noise values, look up a biome", every biome gets a *weight* at every point, and the terrain height is the weighted sum over all eight. Measured across six kilometres, **0.02%** of all steps are steeper than three blocks. Plus huge mountains, canyons and caves.

**The world reacts.** Blocks fall. Trees topple over as one rigid body instead of vanishing. Saplings regrow. Water flows and reflects. And there's a rule I'm pretty happy with: **what you place from crafted materials supports itself, what grew there obeys gravity.** Build a wall out of dirt and watch it collapse; build it out of planks and you get a balcony.

**Crafting and building.** 195 block types, 202 items, 89 recipes across four stations (hand / campfire / workbench / furnace). Five tool tiers from wood to crystal. Doors, ladders, chests, glass with its own render pass, and a tent you can sleep in.

**Tech.** Godot 4.7 (Forward+), pure GDScript. 342 `.gd` files, roughly 105,000 lines, 8 shaders. Hand-written voxel mesher. Everything you see is generated from code — **no imported assets at all**, no textures, no models, not even the title screen. Every shape is a box or a wedge, every colour is a number in a palette.

# About the "vibecoded" part

Written with **Claude (Claude Code)**, but the setup matters more than the model. There's an **MCP server for Godot** hooked straight into the engine, so the AI can start the game, read the scene tree, simulate input, read the console — and **take screenshots of the running game and look at them itself**.

That's the part that stops it from being fancy autocomplete. Example: my player character turned into a solid white blob during the hit-flash and lost all its internal detail. Not a single test caught it — every number was correct. It only showed up because a capture script took a screenshot and someone actually looked. Same story with holes in buildings and a campfire sitting one block too deep in the floor.

So there are **42 automated headless test runs** in the repo now, plus about **190 auto-generated screenshots**, because those catch completely different classes of bugs. A test tells you the hitbox is the right size. Only a picture tells you whether you can tell *who's coming at you* from twenty metres away.

Honest take on the AI thing: it's very good at carrying a decision all the way through, including tests and docs. It's useless if you let it make the decision. The architecture, the constraints, the "what am I deliberately *not* building" list — that's still design work, and no amount of prompting does it for you.

# 

That's the state after a week. I'll post updates as it goes, and a playable build isn't far off.

**If you've got questions, ask away** — happy to go into the voxel mesher, the biome blending, the save format, or what it's actually like working on a Godot project with an AI agent. :)

comments.body: I’m doing something similar in Unreal. Unfortunately my game uses a very popular IP so I won’t be releasing it, it’s really just for me.

comments.author: Brewgazer
comments.body: Looks like you pay attention to detail and care, hmu in dm and I’ll invite you to a discord server with people who are the same

comments.author: CaterpillarLow3756
comments.body: The visual feedback loop via MCP is definitely the secret sauce here. Giving the agent eyes on the actual running build to catch rendering bugs that unit tests miss is huge, especially for procedural voxel stuff. Did you run into many context window limits juggling that many \`.gd\` files and screenshots in Claude Code, or did you have a specific workflow to keep it focused on isolated systems?

replies.author: Veelgez
replies.body:
Yeah, I write pretty much everything directly without using predefined prompts or anything like that. I always review what Claude does afterward and go through the code myself. So far, that approach has worked best for me.  
I think the important part is being very specific when telling Claude or Codex what you actually want, how you want it implemented, and what the technical requirements are. Unfortunately, a lot of people struggle with that because they don’t have enough technical understanding to properly communicate what they want to the AI.
